quiz.question: How does trust usually hold up best in a friendship?
choices: When it's earned slowly through consistent small moments
When it's built instantly by sharing everything right away
quiz.explanation: Sharing something deeply personal with someone you barely know can feel like a shortcut to closeness, but it often isn't earned yet. Trust built gradually through consistent small moments tends to hold up much better.

quiz.question: Does being a good friend mean always being available?
choices: No, protecting some of your own time and energy is healthy
Yes, a good friend must always be available
quiz.explanation: Being a good friend doesn't mean dropping everything every time someone wants your attention. Protecting some of your own time and energy is part of a sustainable friendship, not a betrayal of it.

quiz.question: What's worth paying attention to in a friendship's balance?
choices: A long-term pattern of one-sided effort
Whether every single week is perfectly equal
quiz.explanation: A single week where you did more of the reaching out doesn't mean much on its own. It's a long-term pattern, like always being the one to text first for months, that's actually worth noticing.

quiz.question: What does self-respect look like within a friendship?
choices: Being willing to voice disagreement or discomfort
Always going along with a friend to avoid conflict
quiz.explanation: Respecting yourself in a friendship means being willing to say 'actually, I don't agree' instead of always going along to avoid friction. A friendship that only works when you suppress your opinions isn't fully honest.

quiz.question: Why might sharing something vulnerable too quickly with someone you barely know backfire?
choices: It can feel like a shortcut to closeness that hasn't actually been earned
It always guarantees instant closeness
quiz.explanation: Telling someone you just met your deepest worries can feel bonding in the moment, but that closeness hasn't actually been built yet. Trust usually needs time and small proven moments first.

slides.title: Repairing a friendship after conflict
slides.text: Not every disagreement has to end a friendship — a real conversation about what happened, without rehashing every old grievance, can often repair things. For example, having one honest, calm conversation about a specific fight — instead of avoiding each other for weeks — often clears the air faster than either person expects.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a friend had a disagreement. Does every disagreement have to end the friendship?

options.label: No — a real conversation can often repair it
options.outcome: Exactly right! Not every disagreement has to end a friendship — a real, honest conversation can often repair it.

options.label: Yes, any disagreement means the friendship is over
options.outcome: A disagreement doesn't automatically end a friendship — talking it through can often repair it.

options.label: Disagreements should always just be ignored forever
options.outcome: Ignoring a disagreement forever doesn't resolve it — having a real conversation works much better.

slides.title: Recognizing toxic patterns
slides.text: Instead of judging a friendship from one bad moment, look for repeated patterns: frequent put-downs, pressure, dishonesty, using you only when they need something, or leaving you consistently anxious or drained. Repeated behavior matters more than one difficult day.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend consistently puts you down in front of others, then apologizes privately each time, but the pattern keeps repeating. What should you recognize?

options.label: This is a repeating toxic pattern, not just occasional bad moments
options.outcome: Exactly — a repeated pattern, even with apologies in between, is different from an isolated bad moment. Recognizing the pattern matters more than any single apology.

options.label: Each apology means it's completely fine now
options.outcome: A sincere apology matters, but if the same hurtful behavior keeps repeating, it's a pattern worth addressing directly, not just forgiving each time.

options.label: You're overreacting since they always apologize
options.outcome: Recognizing a repeated pattern of hurtful behavior isn't overreacting — it's an important thing to notice and address.

slides.title: Resisting pressure to exclude someone
slides.text: Peer pressure to leave someone out or join in on unkind behavior can be hard to resist, but choosing not to participate — even quietly — matters. For example, not joining in when a group starts excluding or mocking someone, even if you don't openly object, is a meaningful choice not to add to the harm.

widgetConfig.scenario: A group starts excluding or mocking someone. What's a meaningful choice, even without openly objecting?

options.label: Choosing not to participate
options.outcome: Exactly right! Not joining in when a group starts excluding or mocking someone, even if you don't openly object, is a meaningful choice not to add to the harm.

options.label: Joining in to fit in with the group
options.outcome: Joining in to fit in adds to the harm — choosing not to participate, even quietly, matters a lot.

options.label: Not participating never actually matters
options.outcome: Not participating actually matters quite a bit — it's a meaningful choice not to add to the harm, even without openly objecting.

slides.title: Handling jealousy without damaging trust
slides.text: Feeling a flicker of jealousy when a friend succeeds at something you wanted for yourself is normal — the difference between a healthy friendship and a strained one is often what you do with that feeling. For example, privately acknowledging you feel a little envious, while still congratulating your friend sincerely, keeps the friendship intact instead of letting an unspoken resentment quietly build up.

widgetConfig.scenario: You feel a flicker of jealousy when a friend succeeds at something you wanted. What keeps the friendship intact?

options.label: Privately acknowledging the feeling while still congratulating them sincerely
options.outcome: Exactly right! Privately acknowledging you feel a little envious, while still congratulating your friend sincerely, keeps the friendship intact instead of letting resentment quietly build up.

options.label: Letting an unspoken resentment quietly build up
options.outcome: Letting resentment quietly build up can damage the friendship — acknowledging the feeling while still congratulating them sincerely keeps it intact.

options.label: Feeling a flicker of jealousy is never normal
options.outcome: Feeling a flicker of jealousy is actually quite normal — what matters is what you do with that feeling.

slides.title: The difference between a bad moment and a bad pattern
slides.text: Everyone has an off day, including good friends, so one frustrating interaction doesn't define a friendship; it's the pattern over time, not a single incident, that matters most.

widgetConfig.scenario: A good friend has one frustrating, off day. Does this define the whole friendship?

options.label: No — it is the pattern over time that matters most
options.outcome: Exactly right! Everyone has an off day, including good friends, so one frustrating interaction doesn't define a friendship — it's the pattern over time that matters most.

options.label: Yes, one bad moment always defines a friendship
options.outcome: One bad moment doesn't always define a friendship — it's the pattern over time that really matters.

options.label: A single incident always matters more than a long-term pattern
options.outcome: A single incident actually matters less than a long-term pattern — one off day doesn't define a whole friendship.

slides.title: When to step back from a friendship
slides.text: It can be reasonable to create distance when a friendship repeatedly feels unsafe, disrespectful, controlling, or exhausting and honest conversations do not improve things. Stepping back can mean less contact, clearer boundaries, or ending the friendship if needed.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friendship has started feeling one-sided and draining, even after you've talked to them about it. What's a healthy next step?

options.label: Give yourself permission to create some distance
options.outcome: That's healthy — you've tried addressing it, and it's okay to protect your own wellbeing by stepping back from a friendship that isn't working.

options.label: Keep trying the exact same approach indefinitely
options.outcome: If talking about it hasn't changed anything, repeating the same approach usually won't either — it may be time to reconsider the friendship.

options.label: Cut them off abruptly without any explanation
options.outcome: An abrupt cutoff can feel like the easy way out, but a calm, clear conversation (even a short one) usually leaves things less messy.

slides.title: Manipulation vs. honest disagreement
slides.text: There's a real difference between a friend honestly disagreeing with you and a friend using guilt, silent treatment, or threats to end the friendship to get their way; learning to notice that difference protects you.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend uses guilt or threats to end the friendship to get their way. Is this the same as honest disagreement?

options.label: No — there is a real difference between manipulation and honest disagreement
options.outcome: Exactly right! There's a real difference between a friend honestly disagreeing with you and a friend using guilt or threats to get their way — learning to notice that difference protects you.

options.label: Yes, these are exactly the same thing
options.outcome: These aren't the same — using guilt or threats to get your way is manipulation, which is very different from honest disagreement.

options.label: Noticing the difference between manipulation and disagreement never matters
options.outcome: Noticing this difference actually matters a lot — it protects you from being manipulated under the guise of disagreement.

slides.title: Addressing conflict directly vs. through others
slides.text: Venting about a disagreement to a mutual friend, instead of talking to the person involved, often makes a conflict worse and drags other people into something that isn't theirs.

widgetConfig.scenario: You vent about a disagreement to a mutual friend instead of the person involved. What's the likely effect?

options.label: It often makes the conflict worse and drags others in
options.outcome: Exactly right! Venting about a disagreement to a mutual friend, instead of talking to the person involved, often makes a conflict worse and drags other people into something that isn't theirs.

options.label: It always makes the conflict resolve faster
options.outcome: Venting to someone else usually doesn't resolve the conflict faster — it often makes things worse and drags others in.

options.label: Venting to someone else never affects a conflict
options.outcome: Venting to someone else actually can affect a conflict quite a bit — it often makes it worse and involves people who shouldn't be dragged in.

slides.title: Apologizing for your part, even in a mutual conflict
slides.text: Most conflicts involve some contribution from both sides, so being willing to own your specific part, even if the other person also did something wrong, tends to resolve things faster.

widgetConfig.scenario: Most conflicts involve some contribution from both sides. What tends to resolve things faster?

options.label: Owning your specific part, even if the other person also did something wrong
options.outcome: Exactly right! Being willing to own your specific part, even if the other person also did something wrong, tends to resolve things faster.

options.label: Waiting for the other person to apologize first
options.outcome: Waiting for the other person to go first can stall things — owning your own part first tends to resolve conflicts faster.

options.label: Owning your part never actually helps resolve a conflict
options.outcome: Owning your part actually helps a lot — it tends to resolve conflicts faster than waiting for the other person.

slides.title: Look for patterns, not labels
slides.text: One rude comment or bad day does not automatically define a whole friendship. Pay attention to repeated behavior over time—how often problems happen, whether the person takes responsibility, and whether things improve after you talk about them.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend has one rude comment or bad day. Does this automatically define the whole friendship?

options.label: No — repeated behavior over time matters more
options.outcome: Exactly right! One rude comment or bad day does not automatically define a whole friendship — pay attention to repeated behavior over time instead.

options.label: Yes, one rude comment always defines a friendship
options.outcome: One rude comment doesn't automatically define a friendship — repeated behavior over time matters much more.

options.label: Patterns over time never matter more than a single moment
options.outcome: Patterns over time actually matter much more than a single moment when judging a friendship fairly.

quiz.question: What often helps repair a friendship after a conflict?
choices: An honest, calm conversation about what happened
Avoiding each other indefinitely
quiz.explanation: One honest, calm conversation about a specific fight, instead of avoiding each other for weeks, often clears the air faster than either person expects. Naming what happened, without dragging up old grievances, gives the friendship room to move forward.

quiz.question: What's a sign of a potentially toxic friendship pattern?
choices: Consistently feeling drained or worse after spending time with them
Feeling happy and supported most of the time
quiz.explanation: Noticing that you consistently feel drained or anxious after spending time with a specific person, rather than just having one bad day, is worth taking seriously. A pattern like that says more than any single hangout does.

quiz.question: What's a meaningful way to resist pressure to exclude someone?
choices: Simply not joining in, even quietly
Joining in so you're not the odd one out
quiz.explanation: Not joining in when a group starts excluding or mocking someone, even if you don't openly object, is a real choice not to add to the harm. It takes quiet courage to step back from something everyone else is doing.

quiz.question: What's the healthy way to handle jealousy toward a friend's success?
choices: Acknowledge the feeling privately, but still support them sincerely
Let the resentment build up silently
quiz.explanation: Privately admitting you feel a little envious when a friend succeeds, while still congratulating them sincerely, keeps the friendship intact. Letting that feeling stay unspoken is what tends to cause real damage.

quiz.question: What matters more in judging a friendship?
choices: The overall pattern over time, not a single off day
Any one frustrating interaction, no matter how rare
quiz.explanation: Everyone has an off day, even good friends, so one frustrating interaction doesn't define a whole friendship. It's the pattern over time that actually tells you something.

quiz.question: Is it okay to distance yourself from a consistently stressful friendship?
choices: Yes, it's a legitimate choice, not a failure
No, you should never step back from any friendship
quiz.explanation: Stepping back from a friendship that's become a consistent source of stress, rather than support, isn't a failure on your part. Choosing to protect your own wellbeing is a legitimate, healthy decision.

quiz.question: What's a sign of manipulation rather than honest disagreement?
choices: Using guilt or threats to end the friendship to get their way
Calmly explaining why they see things differently
quiz.explanation: A friend calmly explaining why they see something differently is honest disagreement. A friend using guilt or threats to get what they want is manipulation, and learning to tell the two apart protects you.

quiz.question: What often makes a conflict worse?
choices: Venting to a mutual friend instead of talking to the person involved
Talking directly to the person you disagree with
quiz.explanation: Venting about a disagreement to a mutual friend, instead of talking to the person actually involved, often makes the conflict worse. It drags other people into something that isn't theirs.

quiz.question: What tends to resolve a mutual conflict faster?
choices: Being willing to own your specific part in it
Waiting for the other person to apologize first
quiz.explanation: Most conflicts involve some contribution from both sides, so owning your specific part, even if the other person also did something wrong, helps break the standoff. Waiting for them to go first often just leaves both people stuck.

quiz.question: What's a healthier response to noticing a toxic pattern in a friendship, over just one bad day?
choices: Taking the repeated pattern seriously
Dismissing it since everyone has bad days sometimes
quiz.explanation: Everyone has an off day, so a single bad moment doesn't need to be a big deal. But a repeated pattern, like always feeling worse after seeing someone, deserves to be taken seriously.

slides.title: Long-distance friendships
slides.text: Friendships can survive moving away or going to different schools, but they usually need more intentional effort — a call, a message, a visit — since you won't just run into each other anymore. For example, scheduling a regular video call with a friend who moved away, instead of hoping you'll naturally stay in touch, keeps a long-distance friendship genuinely alive.

widgetConfig.scenario: A close friend is moving to a different school. Can the friendship survive the distance?

options.label: Yes — friendships can survive distance with some effort
options.outcome: Exactly! Friendships can survive moving away or going to different schools, especially with some ongoing effort from both sides.

options.label: No, moving away always ends a friendship completely
options.outcome: Moving away doesn't automatically end a friendship — it can survive with some effort to stay connected.

options.label: Distance makes effort completely unnecessary
options.outcome: Distance actually makes effort more important, not unnecessary — staying in touch takes a bit of ongoing work.

slides.title: Growing in different directions
slides.text: As people figure out who they are during the teen years, some friendships naturally fade — that's a normal part of growing, not a personal failure on either side. For example, two friends who were inseparable in middle school discovering very different interests and friend groups by the end of high school is a common, normal part of growing up.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two middle-school best friends discover very different interests by the end of high school. Is this a personal failure?

options.label: No — it is a normal part of growing up
options.outcome: Exactly right! As people figure out who they are during the teen years, some friendships naturally fade — that's a normal part of growing, not a personal failure on either side.

options.label: Yes, this always means someone did something wrong
options.outcome: This doesn't mean someone did something wrong — friendships naturally changing as people grow is completely normal.

options.label: Friendships should never naturally change over time
options.outcome: Friendships actually do naturally change over time as people grow — that's a normal part of life, not a failure.

slides.title: Being present: the power of good listening
slides.text: Really listening — putting your phone down, asking questions, and not planning your response while the other person is still talking — is one of the most underrated ways to deepen a friendship. For example, a friend who remembers a hard conversation from weeks ago and checks in about it, unprompted, is showing a kind of attentiveness that most casual friendships never reach.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend remembers a hard conversation from weeks ago and checks in unprompted. What does this show?

options.label: A kind of attentiveness that deepens a friendship
options.outcome: Exactly right! Really listening — remembering and checking in unprompted — is one of the most underrated ways to deepen a friendship, showing attentiveness most casual friendships never reach.

options.label: Nothing — remembering past conversations never matters
options.outcome: Remembering past conversations actually matters a lot — it shows a kind of attentiveness that deepens a friendship.

options.label: Putting your phone down while listening never makes a difference
options.outcome: Putting your phone down and really listening actually makes a real difference in how present and attentive you feel to a friend.

slides.title: Including someone who's new or on the outside
slides.text: Actively including someone who's new, quiet, or often left on the edge of a group takes a small amount of effort but can change how they experience an entire year. For example, texting someone you don't know well to invite them along, instead of assuming they'll ask to join, is a simple way to make a group feel more open.

widgetConfig.scenario: You text someone you don't know well to invite them along, instead of assuming they'll ask to join. What does this do?

options.label: Makes a group feel more open
options.outcome: Exactly right! Actively including someone who's new, quiet, or often left on the edge of a group takes a small amount of effort but can change how they experience an entire year.

options.label: Makes no real difference to anyone
options.outcome: This actually can make a real difference — it can change how someone experiences being part of a group for a long time.

options.label: Including someone on the outside never actually matters to them
options.outcome: Including someone on the outside actually matters a lot to them — it's a small effort that can have a big impact.

slides.title: Making friends outside your usual circle
slides.text: As your interests and identity keep developing through your teen years, some of your best friendships might come from outside your usual friend group — a club, a job, or a shared interest online. For example, a genuine friendship with someone from a completely different social circle can offer a perspective and support that your closer, more similar friends might not.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friendship forms with someone from a completely different social circle. What can this offer?

options.label: A perspective and support your closer friends might not
options.outcome: Exactly right! A genuine friendship with someone from a completely different social circle can offer a perspective and support that your closer, more similar friends might not.

options.label: Nothing valuable beyond your usual friend group
options.outcome: A friendship outside your usual circle actually can offer something valuable — a different perspective and support your usual friends might not.

options.label: Friendships outside your usual circle are never worth pursuing
options.outcome: Friendships outside your usual circle are actually worth pursuing — they can offer perspectives your closer friends might not.

slides.title: Staying friends across big life changes
slides.text: Not just physical distance, but changes like different schools after graduation, new jobs, or different life paths can strain a friendship; the friendships that last are often the ones both people actively choose to keep investing in.

widgetConfig.scenario: Different schools, new jobs, or different life paths can strain a friendship. What keeps it alive?

options.label: Both people actively choosing to keep investing in it
options.outcome: Exactly right! The friendships that last are often the ones both people actively choose to keep investing in, despite big life changes.

options.label: Friendships that last always require no effort at all
options.outcome: Friendships that last actually do require effort — both people actively choosing to keep investing in it is what keeps it alive.

options.label: Big life changes never actually affect a friendship
options.outcome: Big life changes actually can strain a friendship — what keeps it alive is both people actively choosing to invest in it.

slides.title: Making the first move
slides.text: Reaching out first, even though it can feel vulnerable to be the one who initiates, is often exactly what a fading friendship needs to stay alive.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friendship is fading, and reaching out first feels vulnerable. What does a fading friendship often need?

options.label: Someone to reach out first
options.outcome: Exactly right! Reaching out first, even though it can feel vulnerable to be the one who initiates, is often exactly what a fading friendship needs to stay alive.

options.label: Waiting for the other person to always make the first move
options.outcome: Waiting for the other person to always go first can mean the friendship just keeps fading — reaching out yourself is often what's needed.

options.label: Reaching out first never actually helps a fading friendship
options.outcome: Reaching out first actually can be exactly what a fading friendship needs to stay alive, even though it feels vulnerable.

slides.title: Diversifying your friend group by choice
slides.text: Actively seeking out friends with different backgrounds or perspectives than your own tends to broaden how you see the world, not just add more people to your contact list.

widgetConfig.scenario: You actively seek out friends with different backgrounds and perspectives than your own. What can this do?

options.label: Broaden how you see the world
options.outcome: Exactly right! Actively seeking out friends with different backgrounds or perspectives than your own tends to broaden how you see the world, not just add more people to your contact list.

options.label: Nothing — different perspectives never add anything
options.outcome: Different perspectives actually add a lot — they tend to broaden how you see the world.

options.label: Seeking out different perspectives only adds more contacts, nothing more
options.outcome: Seeking out different perspectives actually does more than add contacts — it genuinely broadens how you see the world.

slides.title: Letting go without bitterness
slides.text: When a friendship fades naturally, it's possible to feel grateful for what it was without needing to stay close forever or view the ending as a failure.

widgetConfig.scenario: A long friendship has naturally faded as you both grew in different directions. How should you think about it?

options.label: Appreciate what it was, without needing to stay bitter
options.outcome: That's a healthy, mature perspective — friendships can be meaningful for a season and still end naturally without anyone being at fault.

options.label: Feel angry and blame them for the friendship ending
options.outcome: Natural drifting apart usually isn't anyone's fault — holding onto bitterness tends to hurt you more than it changes anything.

options.label: Pretend you were never really friends at all
options.outcome: Dismissing what was a real, meaningful friendship isn't necessary — you can honor what it was while accepting it's changed.

slides.title: Friendships need shared effort
slides.text: Staying connected usually works best when both people sometimes reach out, make plans, and show interest in each other's lives. The effort will not be perfectly equal every week, but over time it should not feel like only one person is carrying the friendship.

widgetConfig.scenario: You've been the only one reaching out and making plans in a friendship for months. What does this suggest?

options.label: The friendship needs effort from both sides to stay healthy
options.outcome: Exactly — healthy friendships need mutual effort over time. If it's consistently one-sided, it's worth having an honest conversation about it.

options.label: It's totally fine since friendships don't need balance
options.outcome: Lasting friendships generally do need effort from both people — a consistently one-sided dynamic is worth addressing.

options.label: You should just stop trying immediately without talking about it
options.outcome: Before giving up, an honest conversation about the imbalance often helps — some friends simply aren't aware of the pattern.

It never makes any real difference

Half-listening while doing something else
